title: The kingdom splits (1 Kings 12)
hook: a young king ignores the old counselors and the kingdom tears in two

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon, admitting his house could never hold God. Your line was heaven cannot contain you. Which place did you turn toward? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

"Thy father made our yoke grievous." Solomon is dead, and his son Rehoboam has gone to Shechem to be made king. The people come to meet him, and they bring one request, in the King James words: make the heavy yoke your father put on us lighter, "and we will serve thee." That's the deal on the table. Lighten the load, and you have a kingdom. Rehoboam doesn't answer on the spot. He tells them to go away and come back in three days. And in those three days he asks for advice, twice, from two very different tables. Today, the kingdom splits.

First he goes to the old men, the ones who stood before his father Solomon while he lived. Their answer is a paradox: "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever." Serve them today, and they'll serve you for good. Then he goes to the young men who grew up with him. Their answer is the opposite: talk tough. Tell them, "My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins." Tell them, "my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions." The text puts the choice in one plain line: he "forsook the counsel of the old men." Notice the order. He asked the old ones first. He heard the answer. Then he set it aside and asked again, this time of the friends he grew up with. On the third day he gives the people the young men's speech, word for word. And the people answer with a cry that tears the kingdom: "What portion have we in David? ... to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David." The northern tribes walk away and make Jeroboam their king; only Judah stays with the house of David. The text holds two things together here. Rehoboam made a choice. And, it says, "the cause was from the LORD," fulfilling a word a prophet had already spoken. Readers weigh those two lines differently. But nobody in the story pretends the choice wasn't his. The old men's advice cost nothing but pride: one soft answer, one lighter yoke. He couldn't pay it.
screen: `HE FORSOOK THE COUNSEL OF THE OLD MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a question to an older table. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one decision in front of you right now. Then bring to mind someone older who has seen more of life than you have: a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a retired coworker, a pastor. Hear, as honestly as you can, what they'd probably say. Then ask yourself the hard question: is that the answer I'm avoiding? If you pray, you can bring both the decision and the person before God. The bell holds the time.
Rehoboam. The young king who heard the old men say be a servant, chose the young men's threat instead, and watched the people go to their tents.
Your line: listen to the old ones. Today, actually ask an elder about something real, and let their answer stand for a full day before you argue with it. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Rehoboam's story as a warning about pride and about choosing advisers who only say what we want, and the old men's counsel to be a servant is sometimes linked to Jesus's teaching on servant leadership.

notes: 'Three days' is from 12:5 and 12:12. 'The northern tribes ... only Judah stays' paraphrases 12:20; the script avoids a tribe count (12:21 also names Benjamin with Judah). Confirm the simplification.
The 12:16 quotation is elided ('...') to skip 'neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse'.
The prophet's earlier word is Ahijah's to Jeroboam (11:29–39), referred to without naming him.
'Readers weigh those two lines differently' leaves the human-choice/divine-purpose question open without ranking.
howItsDone's link to Jesus's teaching on servant leadership (e.g. Mark 10:42–45) is described as 'sometimes'; confirm.
